articles.title: Daniel Cormier takes JON JONES' SIDE after Gable Steveson leaves octagon after Sean Sharaf KNOCKOUT

Cormier also gives Jon Jones his flowers as a coach, saying he was wrong to assume that Jones wasn't good for the role, and he believes that taking the blame for Gable leaving further proves his potential as a coach. DC also gives his quick take on the massive heavyweight title fight between Ciryl Gane and Josh Hokit for the interim belt, which he predicted would happen last week. Hear what Cormier believes is next for Gable, why he will only continue to get better, and where he believes Jon has been a great coach for the young prospect. articles.title: Jon Jones Deserves Some Credit #ufc
articles.description: Chael Sonnen was ready to go after Jon Jones—but then Jon said something that completely changed the conversation. Chael explains why he expected to criticize Jones, only to hear a statement he actually agreed with. Instead of dragging out a situation, Jon advocated for getting an injured fighter medical attention as quickly as possible rather than bringing him back into the center of the Octagon for an interview. Chael says that mindset reflects a different side of Jon Jones, arguing that Jones appears more mature and even more likable now than he was during his fighting career. The conversation also raises a bigger question about UFC post-fight interviews: when a fighter has just suffered a knockout or significant damage, should they really be brought back into the spotlight immediately? Chael breaks down why he believes Jon got this one right—and why that surprised him. #UFC #MMA #JonJones #ChaelSonnen #UFCNews #MMAFighters #UFCInterviews #JonJonesNews

articles.title: Did Ilia Just Accuse Gaethje of Cheating? #ufc
articles.description: Did Ilia Topuria just accuse Justin Gaethje of cheating? Chael Sonnen breaks down Ilia’s recent comments about Gaethje’s gloves and explains why he doesn’t necessarily interpret them as a serious accusation. According to Chael, Ilia may have been making a tongue-in-cheek comment about how hard Gaethje hits rather than claiming there was actually something illegal on or inside the glove. Either way, the comment has created exactly what a rematch needs: conversation. With Ilia Topuria and Justin Gaethje seemingly headed toward another fight, Chael explains why this unexpected back-and-forth could actually be useful for building interest in the matchup. Was Ilia making an accusation—or giving Gaethje a compliment? Chael breaks down what he thinks Ilia really meant. #UFC #MMA #IliaTopuria #JustinGaethje #ChaelSonnen #UFCNews #UFCRematch #MMA News

articles.title: Tsarukyan Is a 4-to-1 Favorite Over Gaethje?!
articles.description: Arman Tsarukyan is a four-to-one favorite. Justin Gaethje is plus three-to-twenty-five. Let me tell you what four-to-one actually means, because it doesn't just reflect confidence in your athlete winning. It represents dominance, and not just dominance, but a finish. If you ever bet a guy at four-to-one, bet the finish. That is what the number is telling you. Four-to-one is very uncommon in title fights. To find anything like it you have to go back to Sean Strickland as a six-to-one dog against Israel Adesanya. And here is the thing about Justin Gaethje. His two biggest moments, the interim title over Tony Ferguson and the undisputed title over Ilia Topuria, both came because he was overlooked. Tony didn't know what kind of fight it would be until it was going. Neither did Ilia. Gaethje's secret superpower is moving forward when most men would stop, and opponents buy into that at their own peril. But here is the twist. articles.title: Jon Jones vs Daniel Cormier: The Brawl, The Hearing & The $50,000 Fine (12 Years Ago Today)
articles.description: Jon Jones vs Daniel Cormier: The Brawl, The Hearing & The $50,000 Fine (12 Years Ago Today) On September 23, 2014, the Nevada Athletic Commission ruled on the UFC 178 media-day brawl between Jon Jones and Daniel Cormier. Hours before the Aug. 4 face-off, Cormier told MMA Weekly he would "attack him the whole time." Then the two men touched foreheads on stage, Cormier shoved, Jones swung, and both went off the stage into the MGM Grand lobby. Eight days later Jones withdrew injured and UFC 178's main event collapsed — but Nevada still wanted answers. At the hearing, Jones told commissioners "I made us all look bad… as a man I sit here to accept them," and admitted the brawl cost him his Nike sponsorship. Cormier argued self-defense — "a reaction to him putting his head on mine" — and said he had no Nike deal to lose. The commission's ruling: no suspension for either man. Jones was fined $50,000 with 40 hours of community service; Cormier $9,000 with 20 hours. The motion passed unanimously. Outside the room, Cormier called it fair. They finally fought at UFC 182 on January 3, 2015. Jones won by unanimous decision. articles.title: Michael Morales Doesn't Need Ian Garry
articles.description: Ian Garry and Michael Morales have verbally agreed to fight, and I have got to tell you, Morales would be making a massive mistake. Garry lost his title bid to Islam Makhachev at UFC 330 in August. Morales was the backup fighter that night, and now the unbeaten Ecuadorian sits on the cusp of a title shot. Here is the history lesson. Only two fighters in the history of this sport have weighed in as backup fighters and not gotten an immediate title shot. If Morales fights Garry instead of waiting for Islam, he becomes the third man to drop the bag. Garry is zero and one in twenty-six. Morales is nineteen and oh. That is the whole negotiation. I have beaten nineteen men straight. You are oh and one in the last thirty days. Drop the mic and walk out the door. Now do not misunderstand me. Garry is doing everything right. Coming off a loss, rebounding into a main event against the number one contender is exactly how you play this game. Even if he is a complete narcissist, and I would know, I can spot my own. But a tweet is not a press conference. It is not Ariel's show. It is not sitting down with Uncle Chael. And whoever leaked that private text exchange between these two is out of the club forever. You never reveal what was shared in private. If Morales wants to stick it to Garry, here is how. Do not give him the fight. Your job as a performer is the biggest paycheck against the easiest opponent, and the money is the same either way. Wait for Islam. Cash in the promise Dana made you at Madison Square Garden. articles.title: Jon Jones Did the Right Thing
articles.description: I have spent years waiting for Jon Jones to give me a reason to bury him on camera, and the man keeps making it impossible. At UFC 331, Sean Sharaf knocked out Gable Steveson in twelve seconds, the third fastest heavyweight finish in UFC history. Before Bruce Buffer could even announce it, Jones pulled his fighter out of the cage and took him backstage. The Crypto.com Arena crowd booed. Gable caught all the heat. Then Jones stepped in front of it on X: it was my decision, the first time I'd ever been in that spot, and my only concern was getting my friend to the back to make sure he was okay. He praised Gable's work ethic, said he'll be back, and believes he'll be one of the best heavyweights in the UFC. I showed up ready to embarrass the whole lot of them, the retirement, the coaching gig at Real American Freestyle, all of it. Instead, I watched Jones turn out to be an excellent coach, saw the genuine bond he has with Gable, and watched him absorb the backlash his athlete would have taken. That's what a corner is supposed to do. A guy gets knocked out cold, you don't stand him up for a photo op, you get him to the back. Jones is sensitive to social media and knew he'd get roasted. He did it anyway. It pains me to say it, but Jon Jones was right. articles.title: What Is Ilia Saying About Gaethje's Gloves?
articles.description: Ilia Topuria finally broke his silence, and the internet decided to read him like a legal document. So let me do a little damage control, because I think I know what the man actually meant. Topuria lost to Justin Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 on the White House lawn, then said nothing for weeks. Nothing about moving to a new continent, building a brand-new gym, a year-plus layoff, or fighting five rounds against your favorite fighter's favorite fighter. The man had five verifiable excuses and never used a single one. Then he posted that next time he'd make sure they check Gaethje's gloves so nothing weird ends up on them, and everybody screamed accusation. Here's the thing. English is not his first language, and he said ON the glove, not IN the glove. Read it like a reasonable person and it's a compliment: man, Justin hits so hard I need to check those gloves. I took it the same way I took it in high school when a rival accused me of steroids because my chest looked strong. Andy Foster and the commission inspected everything. Nothing was there. And whether you take him literally or not, the whole saga gave this rematch the back-and-forth it was missing. So be a literalist if you want. The reaction to Gable Steveson’s loss tells Chael Sonnen a lot about how long someone has been watching combat sports. One loss does not mean Gable is finished. History is filled with elite fighters who suffered setbacks and came back better. For Chael, the more interesting question is what Gable should take from the experience. Gable entered MMA as one of the hottest prospects the sport has ever seen, with an elite wrestling résumé and expectations unlike almost anyone before him. But there’s a trap that great wrestlers can fall into when transitioning to MMA: believing they need to prove how well-rounded they’ve become. Chael argues they don’t. Your best weapon should remain your priority. Close the distance. Get your hands on your opponent. Put him against the fence. Take him down. If he gets back up, do it again. The striking, submissions, and other skills are there when you need them, but you don’t need to showcase everything you learned in the gym. Sometimes the lesson is much simpler: do what made you great.
